messages.subject: Re: RJMCMC Proposal Ratio
parts:
Remy, good question.  For a complete understanding, yes, understanding how the Metropolis-Hastings acceptance probability is calculated, to correctly induce the desired stationary distribution (specifically, the posterior distribution) of the Markov chain would be helpful.  But for a short summary:

acceptance probability = [ Pr(proposing opposite-direction-transition) * pi(proposed new state) ] / [ Pr(proposing this transition) * p(current state) ]

where pi() is the target stationary distribution (the posterior distribution).

Say, for example, proposing to *remove* beta2 from the model.  Then, the current state is the current value of beta2, and the proposed new state of beta2 is 0.  Note also that when adding beta2 into the model, we use a Normal proposal distribution with standard deviation of "scale", a fixed value from the sampler "control" list.  Thus:

Pr(proposing this transition) = Pr(proposing 0 as the new value of beta2) = 1, since when we remove beta2, it's necessary that it transitions to a value of 0.
Pr(proposing opposite-direction-transition) = Pr(proposing the newly proposed value of beta2) = N(0; proposed_value, scale)
acceptance probability of removal = [ N(0; proposed_value, scale) * pi(proposed new state) ] / [ 1* pi(current state) ]

Note in your summary, you left out the pi() terms, which are the variables called "currentLogProb" and "proposalLogProb" in the RJindicatorSampler function.

Similar logic holds in the opposite direction, for the acceptance probability of *adding* beta2 into the model.

For much better explanations, see also:
Green, Peter J. "Reversible jump Markov chain Monte Carlo computation and Bayesian model determination." Biometrika 82.4 (1995): 711-732.
Green, Peter J., and David I. Hastie. "Reversible jump MCMC." Genetics 155.3 (2009): 1391-1403.

I hope this helps.  Back to working on my own seminal paper now.

Cheers,
Daniel


On Wed, Feb 8, 2023 at 1:28 PM Remy MacDonald <remyn...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hello,

I am looking at the reversible jump MCMC (RJMCMC) example provided here:

https://r-nimble.org/writing-reversible-jump-mcmc-in-nimble

and I am trying to understand the choice for the proposal ratio in the RJindicatorSampler function. In this example, if we propose removing beta2 then the proposal ratio is N(0; mean=beta_current, sd=sigma) and if we propose adding beta2 then the proposal ratio is 1/N(0; mean=beta_proposed, sd=sigma). Is there a simple explanation for this or would it require a deep understanding of the theory behind RJMCMC?

Thank you in advance!

Remy
